title: Birbal and the Snake Charmer
summary: A boastful snake charmer claims his cobras are entirely under his magical control. Birbal shows the court why playing with treachery always ends in ruin.
full_text:
A famous snake charmer named Ustad Madari arrived at the court of Emperor Akbar, carrying three wicker baskets containing lethal King Cobras. He played his gourd flute (pungi), and the hooded serpents swayed, hissed, and bowed their heads to the rhythm of his music.

The snake charmer boasted: 'Your Majesty, these serpents are my obedient children! Through ancient spells, I have removed all malice from their hearts! They will never bite me, for they love their master!'

Akbar was fascinated and remarked to Birbal: 'Is it not marvelous, Birbal? Even deadly cobras can be tamed by art and love!'

Birbal shook his head with grave wisdom:

'Sire, a cobra's nature is poison. It sways to the motion of the flute, not to love. A man who plays with venomous serpents is merely living on borrowed time.'

The snake charmer scoffed at Birbal's warning, boasting that he had slept with snakes for thirty years.

A month later, news reached the court that Ustad Madari had been bitten on the neck by his favorite cobra while feeding it milk, and had died within minutes.

Akbar remembered Birbal's warning with a shudder: 'Birbal, your prediction was tragically accurate.'

Birbal said with quiet sadness:

'Sire, this is a lesson not merely about serpents, but about statecraft and human companions.

'A ruler who surrounds himself with treacherous, corrupt flatterers, believing he can tame them with gifts and titles, is like that foolish snake charmer. You may feed milk to a viper and play sweet music for years, but when the moment comes, a poisonous soul will invariably strike according to its nature.

'A wise emperor eliminates venomous men from his court before their fangs find his throat.'

Akbar took the lesson deeply to heart, using it to purge corrupt ministers from the imperial administration.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
